## Where This Fits
**The course's third mathematical peak (Appendix C, point 1: W3, W6, W8), and the week that turns W7's arrow around.** W7 asked where the prior lives in $P(\ell \mid \mathbf{X})$; this week asks about $P(\mathbf{X} \mid \ell)$. One line of text has countless legitimate readings — rate, pauses, pitch contour, timbre, breath — so TTS is not a regression problem but the problem of **drawing one sample from a conditional distribution**. Treat it as regression and the answer is the average of all readings: W2's "over-smoothed predicted spectrum" (the second of the three reconstruction losses, the cell W2 Demo 2 left for this week) is what that average sounds like. One question runs through the week: **in a TTS system, where does the decision "which reading" live — who decides the length, who generates the variation, who renders the waveform, and how much does each decision delay the first packet of sound?** Ten years of history can be read along these four sub-questions: Tacotron handed the length to attention (which collapses), FastSpeech to a duration predictor (which needs an aligner as its teacher — W3's Viterbi returns), the codec LM to the autoregressive stop symbol (the half of W7's "the decoder does not know when to stop" returns), and flow matching simply **requires the length up front** (E2 / F5 estimate it from the reference audio and the character count). The variation question has only two answers — autoregression over W6's discrete tokens (W7's prior $P(\ell)$ becomes $P(\mathbf{k} \mid \ell)$: the prior now *generates sound*, which is what W7's closing slide promised), or a velocity field that carries noise to data on continuous mel / latents (**the flow-matching derivation is completed this week**: why CNFs are hard → conditional paths → why the conditional field can stand in for the marginal one → ODE sampling → CFG → straightening and one-step generation; W9's RL post-training and W13's streaming generation are built on it). The waveform question is the vocoder — W6's $\mathcal{L}_{\text{adv}}$, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{feat}}$ and discriminators $\Phi_j$ return unchanged (HiFi-GAN is the decoder half of a codec trained on its own), and W2's phase returns as the iSTFT family of vocoders that predict magnitude and phase directly. The latency question adds up the waiting time of the four decisions and fills in the **TTS first packet** cell of W1's budget.

The second thread is **where the two paradigms end up in a dialogue system**. An autoregressive codec LM streams by construction (each token can go to the decoder as it appears), and its output side is the same kind of thing as W11's audio-native LM and W13's full-duplex models — after W11, TTS is no longer a separate module but the LM's own output stream. Flow matching gives high quality with single-digit NFE, but it generates a whole segment at once and is non-causal: to stream it must be chunked, paying the train / inference mismatch of W4's streaming encoders in the other direction. The mainstream systems of 2026 put **one of each on its own layer**: an AR model decides *what to say and when* (single-codebook semantic tokens in the CosyVoice family; dual-track, multi-codebook in Qwen3-TTS) and a flow / MeanFlow decoder decides *what it sounds like* (token → mel or token → waveform in 2 or even 1 NFE); a parallel line swaps the discrete tokens for continuous latents with a small flow head at every AR step (MELLE, CuteTTS). This week puts them on one table of "where each of the four decisions lives" and does not pick a side.

Where the three course-long axes sit this week. **Representation:** the output side of TTS walks through every representation from W2 to W6 — Tacotron / FastSpeech generate mel (W2's 80 bins at $\Delta = 10$ or 12.5 ms), VITS emits the waveform directly, VALL-E generates W6's RVQ tokens $k_{t,i}$ (EnCodec, 75 Hz × 8 levels), the CosyVoice family generates ASR-supervised single-codebook tokens (25 Hz from CosyVoice 2 on) and decodes them to mel with a flow, CuteTTS generates continuous latents at 12.5 Hz; "who decides the frame rate" is answered this week by **how many steps per second the generative model has to run** (the AR token rate; $R_{\text{tok}}$ of W6, point 7). **Latency:** this week fills the **TTS first packet** cell of W1's budget. W1 Demo 2 measured Kokoro on this machine (non-AR, one shot for the whole sentence, iSTFT output) at a p50 of 124 ms; for an AR codec LM the first packet ≈ text preprocessing + the tokens of the first chunk ($C$ tokens, one step each) + $N_{\text{FE}}$ decoder passes over that chunk + vocoder + playout buffer; for whole-utterance flow matching the first packet equals the time to generate the whole utterance and grows linearly with its length. **Supervision:** paired (text, speech) is the only supervision this week, but three data scales sit side by side — tens of hours of one speaker (the LJSpeech era of Tacotron / FastSpeech), 60,000 hours of unlabelled speech with ASR transcripts (VALL-E's LibriLight), hundreds of thousands to millions of in-the-wild hours (Emilia's 100k, Qwen3-TTS's 5M); RL post-training (W9) and preference data are a fourth, only previewed this week.

Three concrete points on the local-language thread. (1) **Text input for Taiwanese is not a solved problem** — characters with several readings, two romanisations (Tâi-lô and POJ), and **tone sandhi** (the citation tone survives only at the end of a phrase; every syllable before it changes tone by rule): a phoneme-input system needs a G2P that applies sandhi, while a character-input system (the E2 / F5 family) leaves sandhi to be learned from data — and Taiwanese TTS corpora are more than two orders of magnitude smaller than Mandarin ones (). (2) **MMS-TTS has VITS models for `nan` (Min Nan) and `hak` (Hakka)** (trained on New Testament readings by a single speaker; neither model card states the input orthography, but `vocab.json` does: the 48 symbols of `nan` are Latin letters plus the diacritics of Pe̍h-ōe-jī — **the input is romanised Taiwanese, not characters**; the 43 symbols of `hak` include ṳ and f / v / y, i.e. Hakka Pha̍k-fa-sṳ; which Hakka accent it speaks has to be heard, Demo 3); Whisper has neither language (W7). So character input must first pass through a Taiwanese G2P (multiple readings, tone sandhi) — the gap between "a model exists" and "it is usable" is orthography and accent, a point to make in class. (3) **Is tone still in the token?** W6 cited evidence at the SSL-unit level (Osakuade & King 2026: units carry tone), but whether the **ASR-supervised semantic tokens** that mainstream 2026 TTS uses (the S3 family) preserve tone, and how much, this outline found no direct evidence for; it is marked as a prediction **to be verified**: Mandarin ASR transcripts distinguish tones by character, so the supervision carries tone; Taiwanese has little ASR data, so its tokens may fail to learn the seven tones and sandhi — W9's voice cloning and W12's turn-taking each return to this (the thread archived as 9a).

## Learning Objectives
1. Write TTS as sampling from $P(\mathbf{X} \mid \ell)$, explain why regressing to the conditional mean yields an over-smoothed spectrum (the source of W2's third reconstruction loss), and read the evolution concatenative → SPSS → Tacotron → FastSpeech / VITS → codec LM → flow matching as the history of three decisions moving house: who decides the length, who generates the variation, who renders the waveform.
2. Write the three solutions to the length-and-alignment problem of TTS — attention (why it repeats and skips), a duration predictor with a length regulator (whose teacher is MFA or MAS; MAS is W3's Viterbi restricted to monotonic alignments), and the autoregressive stop symbol — and explain why flow matching must know the total length in advance and how E2 / F5 estimate it.
3. Derive the conditional flow-matching objective: from why the CNF log-likelihood is expensive, to the step "regressing on the conditional field has the same gradient as regressing on the marginal field", write $\mathbf{X}_\tau$ and the target velocity $\mathbf{X}_1 - \mathbf{X}_0$ for the linear (OT) path and Euler sampling; explain that the velocity field and the diffusion score differ by a linear conversion, give the CFG formula and what too large a $w$ does to speech, and say why rectified flow's "straightening" and MeanFlow's average velocity bring the NFE down to 1–2.
4. Write VALL-E's AR (first level) + NAR (remaining levels) factorisation, explain that in-context voice cloning is "continuing the prompt's tokens", and compare the three 2026 variants (single-codebook semantic tokens + a flow decoder, dual-track multi-codebook, continuous latents + a flow head) by where each places the four decisions; derive the missing-word, repetition and non-stopping failures of AR TTS from "the stop symbol is learned".
5. Write HiFi-GAN's three losses (in W6's notation), say why the MPD looks at periods and what removing each term sounds like; explain how iSTFT vocoders (Vocos) sidestep phase wrapping, and why the vocoder is often the most expensive stage on device.
6. Write the first-packet latency of an AR and of a NAR system in W1's notation, compute it from numbers (NFE, chunk length, token rate, time per forward pass), fill in W1's budget table, and explain why chunk-aware flow matching must see the chunk mask at training time.

## References
**Evolution and alignment**
- Wang et al. (14 authors), **Tacotron: Towards End-to-End Speech Synthesis**, Interspeech 2017, pp. 4006–4010 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2017-1452; arXiv:1703.10135) — the first end-to-end seq2seq TTS; Griffin-Lim for the waveform (§3.4); attention "gets stuck" (§5.1); the pair "word skipping and repeating" is FastSpeech's name for it (§1)
- Shen et al. (13 authors), **Natural TTS Synthesis by Conditioning WaveNet on Mel Spectrogram Predictions** (Tacotron 2), ICASSP 2018, pp. 4779–4783 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP.2018.8461368; arXiv:1712.05884) — autoregressive mel regression with location-sensitive attention plus a WaveNet vocoder; the abstract's MOS of 4.53 against 4.58 for human speech is where "quality is close to saturation" comes from
- van den Oord et al., **WaveNet: A Generative Model for Raw Audio**, arXiv:1609.03499 (2016, preprint) — the first neural vocoder, sample-by-sample autoregression; too slow to deploy, which motivated the GAN vocoders
- Ren et al., **FastSpeech: Fast, Robust and Controllable Text to Speech**, NeurIPS 2019 (arXiv:1905.09263) — duration predictor + length regulator; the teacher is the attention of an autoregressive model
- Ren et al., **FastSpeech 2: Fast and High-Quality End-to-End Text to Speech**, ICLR 2021 (arXiv:2006.04558) — durations from MFA; pitch and energy as variance information
- Kim, Kim, Kong & Yoon, **Glow-TTS: A Generative Flow for Text-to-Speech via Monotonic Alignment Search**, NeurIPS 2020, pp. 8067–8077 (arXiv:2005.11129) — MAS: dynamic programming over monotonic alignments, no external aligner; Key Math 2 follows it
- Kim, Kong & Son, **Conditional Variational Autoencoder with Adversarial Learning for End-to-End Text-to-Speech** (VITS), ICML 2021, PMLR 139 (arXiv:2106.06103) — one-stage, waveform output; stochastic duration predictor; the base of MMS-TTS and the Kokoro family
- Popov, Vovk, Gogoryan, Sadekova & Kudinov, **Grad-TTS: A Diffusion Probabilistic Model for Text-to-Speech**, ICML 2021, PMLR 139:8599–8608 (arXiv:2105.06337) — the first score-based TTS decoder, MAS alignment; Table 2's 4 / 10 / 100 / 1000 steps is the earliest quantification of the NFE knee
- Mehta, Tu, Beskow, Székely & Henter, **Matcha-TTS: A Fast TTS Architecture with Conditional Flow Matching**, ICASSP 2024, pp. 11341–11345 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP48485.2024.10448291; arXiv:2309.03199) — OT-CFM for TTS, MAS alignment, single-digit NFE; the smallest flow TTS for teaching
- McAuliffe, Socolof, Mihuc, Wagner & Sonderegger, **Montreal Forced Aligner: Trainable Text-Speech Alignment Using Kaldi**, Interspeech 2017 (DOI 10.21437/Interspeech.2017-1386) — the duration teacher of FastSpeech 2 and Voicebox; W3's HMM-GMM forced alignment
- Zen, Tokuda & Black, **Statistical Parametric Speech Synthesis**, Speech Communication 51(11):1039–1064 (2009; DOI 10.1016/j.specom.2009.04.004) — the overview of the SPSS era; over-smoothing was already named there as one of three quality-degrading factors (§3.3, §3.3.3 of the authors' version: "muffled")
- Hunt & Black, **Unit Selection in a Concatenative Speech Synthesis System Using a Large Speech Database**, ICASSP 1996, vol. 1, pp. 373–376 (DOI 10.1109/ICASSP.1996.541110) — the concatenative representative
- Tan, Qin, Soong & Liu, **A Survey on Neural Speech Synthesis**, arXiv:2106.15561 (2021, preprint); book version **TAN** (Springer 2023)

**The flow-matching / diffusion route**
- Lipman, Chen, Ben-Hamu, Nickel & Le, **Flow Matching for Generative Modeling**, ICLR 2023 (arXiv:2210.02747; no Comments line on arXiv, acceptance confirmed on OpenReview) — the main text for this week's derivation: Eq. 5 (FM), Eq. 9 (CFM), Theorem 1 (the marginal field generates the marginal path), Theorem 2 (CFM and FM have the same gradient), the OT path of §4.1 Example II (Eq. 20–21)

- Liu, Gong & Liu, **Flow Straight and Fast: Learning to Generate and Transfer Data with Rectified Flow**, ICLR 2023 (arXiv:2209.03003) — linear interpolation and reflow (§2.1); where "straightening holds only at the marginal level" comes from: flow trajectories cannot cross, so the rectified flow "rewires" individual trajectories (§2.1), marginals are preserved (Theorem 3.3), the 1-rectified flow is not straight (§5.2), reflow straightens it further (Theorem 3.7)
- Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, **Building Normalizing Flows with Stochastic Interpolants**, ICLR 2023 (arXiv:2209.15571) — the third independent version of the same idea

- Ho, Jain & Abbeel, **Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models**, NeurIPS 2020, pp. 6840–6851 (arXiv:2006.11239)

- Other streaming / codec-LM TTS systems of 2025–2026: search *streaming TTS interleaved text speech tokens*, *single-codebook speech tokenizer TTS*, *MOSS-TTS*, *VoxCPM*, *IndexTTS* (IndexTTS 2.5 is in W9's references)
